title: Inside a black hole? What the sources predict—and why this route closed

render_contract.target_narration_wpm: 120-135; design at 128, then gate the encoded audio
render_contract.caption_plan: Generate timed sentence captions from the final narration; retain assertion headings and diagram labels so the argument remains legible when muted.

visual_language.motion: slow diagram construction and state transitions only; no decorative particle fields

cards.heading: This route closed because it had no calibrated, identifying target
cards.narration: Could our universe be inside a black hole? It's a personal side-interest — not part of the lab's research programme. We read the original papers to see what they actually predict. One idea gives us a number to check against real stars. For galaxy spin, the sources give no expected size for the effect — and even a perfect measurement couldn't tell us a black hole was the cause. So this route closes. The idea is not declared true or false.

Left: A PERSONAL SIDE-QUESTION · NOT PART OF THE LAB'S RESEARCH PROGRAMME badge above a plain nested-horizon icon, immediately paired with NOT PART OF THE LAB'S RESEARCH PROGRAMME. Centre: PRIMARY SOURCES flow into two branches. Right branch A: A NUMBER WE CAN CHECK. Right branch B: GALAXY SPIN -> NO CALIBRATED TARGET (THE SOURCES GIVE NO EXPECTED SIZE FOR THE EFFECT) + NOT IDENTIFYING BY ITSELF -> ROUTE CLOSED. Animate both branches early enough that stakes, work, and verdict all land by 35 seconds. Keep the exact boundary badge visible from frame one for the full card.

cards.heading: “Black-hole universe” names different proposals, not one model
cards.narration: Here's the first surprise. We found at least five different proposals under this label — black-hole universe, or BHU for short. A closed universe inside a black hole. A collapse that bounces instead of crushing to a point. A universe that inherits its parent's spin. Universes that reproduce, tuning the numbers built into physics. And baby universes with entirely different fingerprints. Five ideas — and no shared prediction. We wrote what we found into a closing record — the document this video reports from.
cards.diagram: G1 sound-off fan. One label BLACK-HOLE UNIVERSE (BHU) fans into five compact tiles that light one-by-one in spoken order: CLOSED UNIVERSE INSIDE A BLACK HOLE; COLLAPSE BOUNCES; INHERITS PARENT'S SPIN; UNIVERSES REPRODUCE AND TUNE PHYSICS; BABY UNIVERSES WITH DIFFERENT FINGERPRINTS. Give each tile a distinct mechanism glyph. Each output arrow ends at a different visible point and no arrows reconverge. Final state holds FIVE IDEAS · NO SINGLE SHARED FORECAST and introduces a document icon labelled CLOSING RECORD · THE DOCUMENT THIS VIDEO REPORTS FROM. No cosmic montage.
on_screen_support: AT LEAST FIVE PROPOSALS IN THIS SURVEY

cards.heading: A test needs a target that can be wrong—and identify the idea
cards.narration: To test an idea, the model has to risk being wrong. It needs a number, a range, or a distinctive pattern that a measurement can miss. And if you find it, it has to point back at that one idea — not at three different ones. In the whole family we surveyed, the closing record found one clean numerical test. It uses neutron stars—the ultra-dense collapsed cores of exploded stars. The ones we can time as they spin are called pulsars, and their mass can be measured.
cards.diagram: Build the central logic that will recur later: MODEL -> TARGET BAND -> MEASUREMENT. First let the measurement miss the band to show CAN BE WRONG. Then let one observation point back toward several possible causes to show NOT IDENTIFYING. Finish with the two requirements: A TARGET THAT CAN BE MISSED and A RESULT THAT IDENTIFIES THE IDEA.
on_screen_support: SPINNING, TIMED NEUTRON STARS ARE PULSARS

cards.heading: One cosmological-natural-selection chain puts a low ceiling on neutron-star mass
cards.narration: One proposal — called cosmological natural selection — says universes have children: every black hole buds off a new universe with slightly different physics. Over many generations, that would tune physics toward making black holes. In the Brown–Lee–Rho chain our record surveyed, the Brown–Bethe maximum neutron-star mass is about one and a half times the mass of our Sun—one point five solar masses. Their paper says a neutron star at approximately two solar masses or above would put that chain in ‘serious doubt or simply falsify’ it. That's a real test — a number that could be proven wrong.
cards.diagram: G2 sound-off family tree and mass ceiling. First draw one parent universe producing black holes; each black hole buds a child universe with a small physics-setting shift. Collapse that lineage into a full mass gauge. A bar labelled POSSIBLE NEUTRON-STAR MASS rises toward a hard lid labelled BROWN–BETHE MAXIMUM ~1.5 M☉. Separately shade the source's approximate M ≳ 2 M☉ regime and place the exact quote inside that region: SERIOUS DOUBT OR SIMPLY FALSIFY — BROWN, LEE & RHO. Make clear this is one proposal's predicted ceiling, not an experiment being run and not a rule shared by every proposal. No unsupported equation-of-state detail.
on_screen_support: “SERIOUS DOUBT OR SIMPLY FALSIFY” — BROWN, LEE & RHO

cards.heading: Measured pulsars have entered the source’s approximately two-solar-mass regime
cards.narration: Weighing a star thousands of light-years away is hard, so every measurement comes with an uncertainty range. Two heavy pulsars matter here. One weighs in at one point nine seven Suns, give or take point zero four — just under two. The other: two point zero eight, give or take point zero seven. At the sixty-eight point three percent level the paper quotes, that one clears two Suns. At the stricter ninety-five point four percent level, the closing record says it does not.
cards.diagram: G3 sound-off full horizontal mass axis from 1.4 to 2.2 M☉. Keep the source's ~1.5 marker and the approximate M ≳ 2 M☉ regime. Row 1 prints DEMOREST: 1.97 ± 0.04 M☉, with its centre below 2.00 and interval crossing 2.00. Row 2 prints FONSECA: 2.08 ± 0.07 M☉ · 68.3%, with that interval above 2.00. Animate the Fonseca interval widening as a non-scaled mode label outside the mass plot changes from 68.3% to 95.4%: the lower side becomes a continuous open-ended gradient that fades through the 2.00 line with no drawn terminus. Retain a separate non-scaled callout: AT 95.4% CREDIBILITY, THE CLOSING RECORD STATES ONLY THAT THE RESULT DOES NOT CLEAR 2.00; NO LOWER-BOUND VALUE IS QUOTED HERE. Hard constraint: draw no 95.4% endpoint, arrow, tick, bracket, marker, whisker, shaded boundary, axis-aligned glyph, or other position-bearing terminus at any scaled mass value. The gradient must have no visible edge that could be read as a lower bound. No inferred bound.

cards.heading: The evidence enters the test regime; the closing record does not call it falsification
cards.narration: Here we have to be careful. Brown, Lee, and Rho gave two possible readings, joined by an ‘or’: a heavy neutron star would put the chain in serious doubt, or simply falsify it. The closing record does not decide which side applies — and neither does this video. The finding is narrower: observations have entered the regime named by the source.
cards.diagram: Keep the mass plot dimmed in the background. Place the exact source disjunction in two equal outlined boxes joined by OR. Stop a measurement arrow before either box and label CLOSING RECORD DOES NOT ADJUDICATE. Highlight only ENTERS THE NAMED REGIME.

cards.heading: The rotating-parent source explicitly says the two handedness counts should differ
cards.narration: A different proposal led to our sky work. If the parent black hole rotates, the child universe inherits its axis. The source says galaxies should tend to align with that axis. It then says clockwise- and counterclockwise-spinning galaxy counts should be different. Our search wasn't chasing a phantom. The claim really is there in the paper — in words. What's missing is any number to go with it.
cards.diagram: Simple rotating-parent cross-section, axis line passing into a child-universe circle, then a field of stylized galaxy disks aligned around that axis. Split count bins CW and CCW with an unequal sign but no invented percentage. Footer: QUALITATIVE SOURCE CLAIM · NO AMPLITUDE SHOWN.

cards.heading: The handedness claim came after the cited data and never became a numerical forecast
cards.narration: But that sentence was added in 2025, after the galaxy studies cited as support. It was not a prediction made before the data—this one came after. The paper gives equations for spinning systems, but not a numerical forecast for galaxy handedness: no expected size, no rule for where or when it should be stronger, no independently predicted direction, and no range that would count as a hit or a miss.
cards.diagram: G5 sound-off timeline and forecast contract. Timeline: CITED GALAXY STUDIES first; HANDEDNESS CLAIM ADDED IN 2025 later. Beneath it, show EQUATIONS FOR SPINNING SYSTEMS as present, then four large empty outlined blanks labelled exactly SIZE? · WHERE/WHEN? · DIRECTION? · PASS-OR-FAIL RANGE?. The blanks pulse once and never fill. End on NOT A PREDICTION MADE BEFORE THE DATA. Do not say the source contains no numbers or equations and do not imply an experiment was run.
on_screen_support: NOT A PREDICTION MADE BEFORE THE DATA
NO EXPECTED SIZE OR PASS-OR-FAIL RANGE FOR HANDEDNESS

cards.heading: A real spin difference would still not identify a black-hole origin
cards.narration: Suppose a controlled survey found a real spin-handedness difference. That would be interesting. But that broad observation would not identify BHU by itself. The same lopsided sky could come from several different causes. Without a fingerprint only a black-hole birth would leave, the measurement can't pick one. A successful measurement is not automatically a successful test of this model.
cards.diagram: The centerpiece identifying-test diagram. One observed node, CW/CCW DIFFERENCE, points backward toward BHU? and OTHER POSSIBLE CAUSES. The backward arrow splits, so the observation cannot select one cause. Do not name or depict specific rival cosmologies. End on the explicit logic MEASUREMENT ≠ IDENTIFICATION.

cards.heading: The spin route fails twice: no numerical target, and no unique signature
cards.narration: The route therefore fails in two independent ways. There's no pass-or-fail range to grade a measurement against — the idea never says how big the effect should be. And without a unique signature, a positive result cannot identify BHU. We could build a trustworthy measurement and still be unable to answer the BHU question. The hunt had a source. It did not have a target.
cards.diagram: G7 sound-off two-column fail-closed comparison. Column A: NO SOURCE-DEFINED PASS-OR-FAIL RANGE—show a finite-precision spin result beside a blank scoring ruler labelled NO PREDICTED SIZE; do not imply that every possible qualitative observation is irrelevant. Column B: NO UNIQUE SIGNATURE—show one observed node with split backward arrows labelled POSITIVE RESULT DOES NOT IDENTIFY BHU. Both columns feed ROUTE CLOSED FOR THIS CAMPAIGN'S SKY-STATISTICS LINE. Keep MEASUREMENT MAY STILL BE TRUSTWORTHY visibly separate. Final line: THE HUNT HAD A SOURCE · IT DID NOT HAVE A TARGET.

cards.heading: Reopen this route only for a calibrated target or a unique signature
cards.narration: What would change the verdict? First, a published calculation that says how big the spin difference should be — with a pass-or-fail range. Or second, a fingerprint only a black-hole birth would leave—not merely the broad fact of spin asymmetry. A confirmed spin asymmetry alone would still not test BHU. This route reopens only when a BHU model supplies a calibrated target or a unique signature.
